steps.title: A hamza out front
body: Form IV's signature is a hamza prefixed to the root, giving the shape أَفْعَلَ — no doubling, no long alif, just أَ added at the front.

Two verbs you already know are Form IV: أَرَادَ ("to want," its present tense أُرِيدُ you've used since your very first "I would like..." phrase) and أَغْلَقَ ("to close"): أَغْلَقَ الرَّجُلُ الْبَابَ, "the man closed the door," present tense يُغْلِقُ.

Form IV often adds a causative sense, similar to Form II — but it's more often built from a plain noun or adjective rather than another verb, or simply lexicalized on its own the way أَرَادَ and أَغْلَقَ are.

steps.title: Form IV in one sentence
steps.intro: Read the sentence, then check what marks it as Form IV. Tap 🔊 to hear it.

steps.title: A form you already knew
steps.prompt: أَرَادَ (to want) starts with أَ. Which form is that?
steps.explanation: أَفْعَلَ prefixes أَ to the root — you've said أُرِيدُ (its present tense) many times without naming this pattern until now.

steps.title: Meaning tendency
steps.prompt: What tendency does Form IV often share with Form II?

options.label: A causative sense — "to make X happen"
A reciprocal sense — doing the action with someone
No human subject is ever possible

steps.explanation: Both II and IV often make a verb causative, though they're built differently — II by doubling, IV by prefixing أَ. (This sentence's own الرَّجُلُ, "the man," is a human subject doing the closing — the opposite of the third option.)

steps.title: Three forms down
steps.message: Form IV — أَ prefixed, often causative like Form II but shaped differently. On to Form V.
